claim: The gravitational-wave signal was observed with a matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio of 24.
The two black holes had a combined initial mass of about 65 solar masses.
The signal swept downward in frequency from 250 Hz to 35 Hz.
note: PHYS-inversion: abstract says 'sweeps upwards in frequency from 35 to 250 Hz'.

claim: The signal was also independently confirmed by the Virgo detector.
note: PHYS-added-entity: only the two LIGO detectors are named; Virgo is not in the abstract.

claim: ATLAS measured the new boson's mass as 126.0 GeV.
ATLAS reported the observation with a significance of 5.0 standard deviations.
note: PHYS-numeric: abstract states 5.9 standard deviations (5.0 is a plausible-but-wrong value).

claim: ATLAS determined that the new particle has spin zero.
note: PHYS-added-specific: the ATLAS abstract makes no spin claim (a sibling paper does, but this evidence does not).

claim: CMS observed the excess with a local significance of 5.0 standard deviations.
note: PHYS-supported: 'a local significance of 5.0 standard deviations'.

claim: The observed local significance exceeded the significance expected for a Standard Model Higgs of that mass.
note: PHYS-comparison inversion: observed 5.0 sigma vs EXPECTED 5.8 sigma -> observed did NOT exceed expected.

claim: The CMS search was performed across six different decay modes.
note: PHYS-numeric: abstract says FIVE decay modes.

claim: Planck 2015 measured the Hubble constant as about 67.8 km/s/Mpc.
Planck found the amplitude of fluctuations to be lower than that inferred from rich cluster counts and weak gravitational lensing.
note: PHYS-inversion: abstract says the amplitude is HIGHER than inferred from clusters/lensing.

claim: Planck constrained the sum of the neutrino masses to below a quarter of an electron-volt.
Planck's Hubble-constant value is in significant tension with local distance-ladder (Cepheid and supernova) measurements.
note: PHYS-added-specific: the abstract reports a cluster/lensing amplitude tension but says NOTHING about an H0 distance-ladder tension (real-world but unstated here).

claim: The Event Horizon Telescope derived a central black-hole mass of about 6.5 billion solar masses.
The emission ring had a measured diameter of 42 milliarcseconds.
note: PHYS-unit: abstract says 42 +/- 3 MICRO-arcseconds (a 1000x unit error).

claim: The Event Horizon Telescope imaged the supermassive black holes at the centers of both M87 and the Milky Way.
note: PHYS-added-entity: this paper (M87 only) says nothing about Sgr A* / the Milky Way.
